text: Thomas Chrowder Chamberlin (/ˈkraʊdər/; September 25, 1843 – November 15, 1928) was an American geologist and educator who founded the Journal of Geology in 1893 and served as its editor for many years. Born in Mattoon, Illinois, he moved to near Beloit, Wisconsin, when he was three years old. His father was a Methodist circuit minister and farmer. Chamberlin attended a preparatory academy before studying at Beloit College, where he received a classical education in Greek and Latin and developed an interest in natural science. While at Beloit, he directed a church choir and participated in athletics and debate. After graduating in 1866, he worked as a teacher and later principal in a high school near Beloit and married Alma Wilson in 1867. From 1868 to 1869, he took graduate courses in geology at the University of Michigan. He then served as professor of natural science at Whitewater Normal School from 1869 to 1873, joined the Beloit faculty in 1873 as professor of geology, zoology, and botany, and became one of several part-time participants in a comprehensive geological survey of Wisconsin. His geological mapping in southeastern Wisconsin, which had thick glacial deposits, led him to identify multiple episodes of glaciation during the Pleistocene, a terminology still in use with minor modifications. In 1875, he started a business with his brother selling spring water. In 1876, he became chief geologist for the Wisconsin geological survey, supervising the completion of a four-volume report in which he authored sections on glacial deposits, Paleozoic and Precambrian bedrock geology, lead-zinc ore deposits, artesian wells, and soils, bringing him national attention and leading to his appointment as head of the glacial division of the US Geological Survey in 1881. He later served as president of the University of Wisconsin from 1887 to 1892. In 1890 and again in 1897, Chamberlin published "The method of multiple working hypotheses," advocating the evaluation of several hypotheses simultaneously, rejecting those inconsistent with data, and concluding with the one supported by evidence—contrasting with the "single ruling theory" that encouraged uncritical acceptance of a dominant hypothesis. The paper is considered a landmark in the scientific method, inspired the strong inference approach, and was reprinted in 1965. In 1892, he accepted a position to organize a geology department at the University of Chicago, where he remained a professor until 1918. From 1898 to 1914, he served as president of the Chicago Academy of Sciences. In 1899, he wrote "An Attempt to Frame a Working Hypothesis of the Cause of Glacial Periods on an Atmospheric Basis," proposing that climate changes could result from variations in atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration, noting that during warming after glacial episodes, oceans release carbon dioxide, accelerating climate improvement. He observed notable fluctuations in the total mass of living matter over geological periods, suggesting that life activity was greatest during times of sea extension and mild climates and least during climatic disruptions, which counteracted the carbon dioxide effects. He concluded that agencies capable of removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere at rates above normal during certain times could cause glaciation, and agencies capable of restoring it during other times could produce mild climates. Chamberlin was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1901 and the United States National Academy of Sciences in 1903. In 1905, he and Forest Ray Moulton proposed the Chamberlin-Moulton planetesimal hypothesis, challenging the Laplacian nebular hypothesis; it received favorable support for nearly a third of a century but fell out of favor by the late 1930s and was ultimately discarded in the 1940s due to incompatibility with Jupiter’s angular momentum, though the idea that planetesimals gradually collided to form planets through accretion remains well-regarded. Chamberlin also concluded that Earth was much older than Lord Kelvin’s estimate of about 100 million years, and his speculations about the Sun’s energy source—derived from internal atomic processes—were prescient. In 1905, he was elected to the American Philosophical Society. In 1909, he and his son Rollin Thomas Chamberlin traveled to the East as members of the Oriental Educational Investigation Commission led by Ernest DeWitt Burton and supported by John D. Rockefeller to assess Eastern regions for potential humanitarian projects of the Rockefeller Foundation. Chamberlin received the inaugural Penrose Gold Medal of the Society of Economic Geologists in 1924 and the inaugural Penrose Medal of the Geological Society of America in 1927. He served as president of the Geological Society of America in 1894. He remained professionally active until his death in Chicago on November 15, 1928. His papers are held at the University of Chicago and Beloit College archives, with the latter also containing the papers of his son, Rollin T. Chamberlin (1881–1948), who was a geologist and later chaired the geology department at the University of Chicago. Buildings are named for him at Beloit College and the University of Wisconsin–Madison, and a house in Burton-Judson Courts at the University of Chicago bears his name. The lunar crater Chamberlin and a Martian crater are named in his honor, and Mount Chamberlin in California is named after him. A 42-ton Precambrian glacial erratic known as the Chamberlin Rock stood on Observatory Hill at the University of Wisconsin–Madison for over 100 years before being moved to a university property on Lake Kegonsa in 2021.
